animals.name: Spotted Salamander
animals.behavior_notes: Spotted salamanders undertake one of the most dramatic amphibian migrations in North America, moving by the hundreds to vernal pools on the first warm rainy nights of late winter to breed. Adults spend the rest of the year entirely underground and are almost never seen.
animals.viewing_tips: On the first rainy night above 45°F in late February or March, visit known vernal pool sites with a red-filtered flashlight — red light is less disruptive to the animals; you may witness dozens to hundreds crossing roads and forest floors in a single evening.

animals.name: Axolotl
parks: Xochimilco Ecological Park (no US NP habitat; captive/zoo only in US)
animals.behavior_notes: Axolotls are critically endangered and not found in any US wild habitat; they are native to lake Xochimilco in Mexico City. In captivity they remain active year-round, foraging slowly along tank or pond bottoms.
animals.viewing_tips: Wild axolotls do not exist in the United States. Your best opportunity is visiting accredited US aquariums such as the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago or the Denver Zoo, which maintain captive populations for conservation purposes.

animals.name: Spring Peeper
animals.behavior_notes: Spring peepers emerge from winter dormancy as early as late February, gathering in large choruses near wetlands, ponds, and woodland pools to breed. Males call loudly at dusk and through the night, producing the iconic high-pitched peeping that signals the arrival of spring.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit shallow woodland ponds or wetland edges after dark on mild, rainy nights in early spring when temperatures are above 40°F. Use a red-filtered flashlight to scan vegetation near the water's edge without disturbing them — hearing them is far easier than spotting these tiny frogs.

animals.name: Atlantic Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Atlantic salmon return to natal rivers in fall to spawn, swimming upstream in aggregations that are visible in shallow, clear streams. Fish are most active during low-light periods as they navigate past riffles and pools.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the Union River or Narraguagus River near Acadia in October; stand on bridges or elevated banks and look for rolling fish or wakes in shallow water. Numbers are very low due to endangered status — patience and local guidance from NOAA are recommended.

animals.name: Chinook Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Chinook salmon, the largest Pacific salmon, push into Olympic Peninsula rivers in fall to spawn, often visible as large dark shapes holding in pools or actively thrashing in shallow gravel redds. Males develop hooked jaws and dark coloration during this period.
animals.viewing_tips: The Hoh and Queets rivers inside Olympic NP offer excellent viewing from riverbanks; polarized sunglasses dramatically improve your ability to spot fish through the water surface. Early morning visits on overcast days reduce glare and improve visibility.

animals.name: Sockeye Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Sockeye salmon turn brilliant red with green heads during their spawning run and crowd Brooks River and other Katmai waterways in massive numbers, making this one of the most spectacular salmon viewing events in the world. The density of fish attracts brown bears, eagles, and other predators.
animals.viewing_tips: Brooks Falls in Katmai is the premier viewing spot — the NPS provides elevated platforms where you can watch salmon leap and bears fish simultaneously. Reserve platform access well in advance through the NPS reservation system, as summer slots fill months ahead.

animals.name: Coho Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Coho salmon enter freshwater rivers in fall, displaying bright red sides and dark backs, and are often seen actively jumping falls or holding in deep pools before moving to spawning gravels. They tend to arrive later than Chinook and are common in smaller coastal streams.
animals.viewing_tips: The Sol Duc and Elwha rivers in Olympic NP are reliable coho viewing sites; walk slowly along stream banks and scan pools with polarized glasses. Coho are skittish — approach quietly and avoid casting shadows on the water.

animals.name: Steelhead Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Steelhead trout are sea-run rainbow trout that migrate into coastal rivers following winter rain events that raise and cool stream flows. They hold in deep, green pools between upstream movements and are often spotted rolling at the surface at dawn.
animals.viewing_tips: Mill Creek and other streams within Redwood NP/SP can be productive after significant rain raises water levels; look for fish from road bridges or gentle bank access points using polarized sunglasses. Avoid disturbing spawning fish in redds — visible gravel depressions with active fish should be observed from a distance.

animals.name: Lake Sturgeon
animals.behavior_notes: Lake sturgeon spawn in late spring over rocky shoals in rivers and lake tributaries when water temperatures reach 55–65°F, sometimes congregating in groups that create visible surface disturbances. Outside spawning, they are bottom-dwellers rarely visible from shore.
animals.viewing_tips: The St. Marys River and Lake Superior tributaries near Pictured Rocks offer the best chance of seeing spawning sturgeon from shore in May; look for large dark forms rolling near rocky shallows at dawn. These fish are state-threatened — maintain respectful distance and do not enter the water near spawning areas.

animals.name: White Sturgeon
parks: Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area
animals.behavior_notes: White sturgeon, the largest freshwater fish in North America, congregate in the Columbia River during spring and can sometimes be seen rolling or breaching near the surface, especially near Bonneville Dam where they gather in large numbers. Adults can exceed 10 feet in length.
animals.viewing_tips: The viewing area and fish ladder at Bonneville Dam (adjacent to the Columbia River Gorge NSA) has an underwater viewing window where sturgeon are commonly seen year-round; the fish hatchery there maintains large display sturgeon. For wild fish, use polarized glasses from elevated banks near deep river pools in spring.

animals.name: Paddlefish
animals.behavior_notes: Paddlefish gather in large river pools and backwaters in spring prior to spawning, sometimes rolling at the surface in ways that reveal their distinctive paddle-shaped rostrum. They are filter feeders that swim slowly with open mouths, making them visible in clear, shallow conditions.
animals.viewing_tips: The Arkansas and Illinois rivers in eastern Oklahoma near Keystone Lake offer the best wild paddlefish viewing; look from elevated riverbanks for rolling fish at low-light periods in spring. The Paddlefish Research Center in Jennings, OK can provide local guidance on current hotspots.

animals.name: Alligator Gar
animals.behavior_notes: Alligator gar are among the largest freshwater fish in North America and are most visible in summer when they surface to gulp air in warm, slow-moving bayous and river backwaters. They often float motionless near the surface like logs, giving patient observers an excellent look at their armored scales and elongated snouts.
animals.viewing_tips: Paddle a kayak or canoe through the slow oxbows and sloughs of the Neches River within Big Thicket NP in early morning before boat traffic increases; scan the surface for large, motionless forms near overhanging vegetation. Alligator gar are not aggressive to humans but are large — enjoy from a respectful distance.

animals.name: Manta Ray
animals.behavior_notes: Giant manta rays are pelagic filter feeders that visit coral reef ecosystems and cleaning stations in the US Virgin Islands, where small fish remove parasites from their bodies. They are most commonly seen gliding effortlessly through clear water, sometimes performing acrobatic somersaults while feeding on plankton near the surface.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling or diving at Buck Island Reef NM provides the best chance of manta encounters; look along reef drop-offs and near cleaning stations on incoming tidal flows when plankton concentrations are highest. Join a licensed dive operator out of Christiansted for guided excursions — mantas are seen most reliably in winter when water clarity is best.

animals.name: Whale Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Whale sharks aggregate in warm Gulf and Atlantic waters during summer months to feed on fish spawn and plankton blooms near the surface. They are slow-moving filter feeders, making them relatively easy to observe once located.
animals.viewing_tips: Book snorkel or dive charters out of Islamorada, FL or offshore Texas platforms near the Gulf where aggregations are documented. Calm, clear days with good visibility are essential for spotting these deep blue giants.

animals.name: Hammerhead Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Great and scalloped hammerheads patrol Florida's warm coastal and reef waters during summer, hunting stingrays and schooling fish in shallow bays and reef edges at dawn and dusk. They are more active and visible near the surface during low-light periods.
animals.viewing_tips: Join a shark dive excursion out of Miami or Key Largo for the best chance of sightings near Biscayne Bay reef edges. Early morning boat trips before afternoon thunderstorms improve both safety and shark activity.

animals.name: Great White Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Great white sharks follow gray seal populations to the outer beaches of Cape Cod from late summer through fall, with peak activity near Nauset and Chatham beaches. They often breach or patrol just beyond the surf zone during midday hours.
animals.viewing_tips: Observation from the shore at Nauset Beach or Chatham is safest and productive; bring binoculars and watch near seal haul-outs. The Atlantic White Shark Conservancy app (Sharktivity) provides real-time sighting data for the area.

animals.name: Bull Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Bull sharks are uniquely adapted to freshwater and regularly move through the brackish and freshwater systems of the Everglades and coastal Florida rivers during warm months. They are most active near river mouths and tidal creeks at dawn and dusk when feeding.
animals.viewing_tips: Kayak or airboat tours through the Everglades' Ten Thousand Islands region offer the best chance of spotting bull sharks in shallow, turbid water. Keep hands inside the boat and maintain a respectful distance if one is observed near the surface.

animals.name: Coelacanth
parks: None — not found in US waters
animals.behavior_notes: Coelacanths are extremely rare, deep-sea fish known from the Indian Ocean and Indonesian waters, with no documented wild populations in US territory. They are nocturnal cave dwellers found at depths of 500–800 feet and virtually impossible to observe in the wild.
animals.viewing_tips: Coelacanths cannot be observed in the wild within the United States — the closest verified wild populations are off South Africa, the Comoros Islands, and Indonesia. The Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C. displays a preserved specimen for educational viewing.

animals.name: Brook Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Brook trout are active in cold, clear Appalachian mountain streams in spring and fall when water temperatures are optimal, often rising to surface flies and insects in early morning. Fall is spawning season, when their brilliant red-orange and blue coloring is most vivid.
animals.viewing_tips: Wade quietly into clear headwater streams in Shenandoah or Great Smoky Mountains early in the morning and look into pools below riffles — brook trout are visible in the shallows. Polarized sunglasses greatly help reduce glare and reveal fish holding near the streambed.

animals.name: Largemouth Bass
animals.behavior_notes: Largemouth bass move into shallow vegetated areas in spring to spawn, making them highly visible near shorelines, lily pads, and submerged structure from March through May. They are ambush predators most active at dawn and dusk when they aggressively feed near the surface.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan the edges of aquatic vegetation in calm coves or lake shallows at dawn with polarized sunglasses — bass are often visible holding just beneath the surface. Warm, sunny days following a cold front when water reaches 60–75°F bring bass activity closest to shore.

animals.name: Monarch Butterfly
animals.behavior_notes: Monarchs gather in large roosts during fall migration, often clustering on trees near coastal areas and open meadows. They feed heavily on late-blooming wildflowers to fuel their long journey to overwintering sites in Mexico.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit coastal refuges and parks along the Atlantic flyway in September and October. Look for roosting clusters on cedar and pine trees at dusk and nectar feeding on goldenrod and asters during midday.

animals.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are active from spring through summer, visiting a wide variety of flowering plants. Males are commonly seen puddling on moist soil and gravel roads to obtain minerals.
animals.viewing_tips: Look for them nectaring on Joe-Pye weed, butterfly bush, and wild bergamot in open meadows and forest edges. Roadsides with mud puddles attract congregating males, making photography especially rewarding.

animals.name: Painted Lady Butterfly
animals.behavior_notes: Painted Ladies are among the most widespread butterflies in the world and undertake long-distance migrations. During peak summer months they are active in open fields and meadows, feeding on thistles, asters, and other composites.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan open meadows and disturbed areas with thistles and wildflowers during warm sunny midday hours. In migration years numbers can be spectacular along mountain foothills and open grasslands.

animals.name: Luna Moth
animals.behavior_notes: Luna Moths are nocturnal and adults do not feed, living only about one week as adults. They are most active on warm, calm nights and are drawn to light sources near forested areas.
animals.viewing_tips: Check outdoor lights near deciduous forests, especially near walnut, hickory, and sweet gum trees, shortly after dark on warm evenings. Early May through June offers the best chances in most of their eastern range.

animals.name: Cecropia Moth
animals.behavior_notes: The Cecropia Moth is North America's largest native moth and is nocturnal. Adults emerge in late spring and are attracted to lights at night, with females releasing pheromones to attract males.
animals.viewing_tips: Check porch lights, mercury vapor lights, and lit windows near wooded areas on warm nights in May and June. Inspect tree trunks and wooden structures at dawn as resting adults may be visible before retreating to cover.

animals.name: American Bumble Bee
animals.behavior_notes: The American Bumble Bee has declined significantly and is now a candidate for federal listing. Workers forage actively in summer on a wide variety of native wildflowers including clovers, coneflowers, and wild bergamot.
animals.viewing_tips: Focus searches on native wildflower prairies and meadows with diverse blooms, especially areas with little pesticide use. Tallgrass prairie preserves in the Midwest represent some of the best remaining habitat for this declining species.

animals.name: Firefly (Eastern)
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Fireflies begin their bioluminescent displays shortly after sunset during warm, humid evenings. Males flash distinctive patterns while flying to attract females resting in low vegetation.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit low-lying meadows, field edges, and forest clearings just after dark on warm, calm, humid nights. Great Smoky Mountains National Park offers a famous synchronous firefly event each June where thousands flash in unison.

animals.name: Periodical Cicada
animals.behavior_notes: Periodical Cicadas emerge en masse after 13 or 17 years underground when soil temperatures reach 64°F. Males produce a deafening chorus to attract females, and the emergence lasts four to six weeks before they die off.
animals.viewing_tips: Check emergence maps and brood schedules to identify active years and locations. Look for emergence holes in the ground and cast nymph skins on tree trunks; adults are easiest to see in deciduous forest edges during warm midday hours.

animals.name: Dragonfly (Common Green Darner)
animals.behavior_notes: Common Green Darners are one of North America's largest and most migratory dragonflies, forming large swarms along coastlines and ridges during fall migration. They hunt actively for insects in open areas near ponds, marshes, and meadows.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit coastal marshes and lakeshores on calm, sunny mornings in late August through October to witness fall migration swarms. Warm days following cold fronts can trigger impressive movements with hundreds visible at once.

animals.name: Praying Mantis
animals.behavior_notes: Praying Mantises reach adult size by late summer and are most conspicuous in August through October when they sit motionless among vegetation waiting to ambush prey. Females grow large and heavy as egg production peaks before first frost.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan tall grasses, goldenrod, and garden shrubs carefully at eye level since their camouflage is excellent. Check flowering plants where pollinators gather, as mantises frequently ambush bees and butterflies visiting flowers.

animals.name: Walking Stick
animals.behavior_notes: Walking sticks are most active at dusk and night when they feed on leaves. During summer months they reach peak adult populations and are easiest to spot on foliage.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan the undersides of oak, cherry, and rose leaves slowly at dusk using a flashlight. Their cryptic camouflage makes them nearly invisible during the day.

animals.name: Tarantula (Desert Blonde)
animals.behavior_notes: Male desert blonde tarantulas roam extensively during late summer and fall in search of mates, making them far more visible than females who rarely leave their burrows. This mating migration peaks between August and October.
animals.viewing_tips: Drive desert roads slowly at dusk during September and October when males cross open ground. Roadsides near Tucson and the Chihuahuan Desert are reliable corridors during peak migration.

animals.name: Black Widow Spider
animals.behavior_notes: Black widow spiders are most active in warm months, building irregular webs in dark, sheltered spots such as rock crevices, wood piles, and desert scrub understory. Females are most visible at dusk when they emerge to tend their webs.
animals.viewing_tips: Use a UV flashlight at dusk to scan rock piles, underbrush, and crevices — their silk glows under ultraviolet light. Never reach into dark spaces without checking first, and observe from a safe distance.

animals.name: American Horseshoe Crab
animals.behavior_notes: American horseshoe crabs mass on Atlantic beaches during full and new moon high tides in May and June to spawn, with females coming ashore and males following close behind. Delaware Bay hosts one of the largest spawning aggregations in the world.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit Delaware Bay beaches such as Slaughter Beach or Reeds Beach during a full or new moon high tide in late May for the peak spectacle. Walk carefully along the wrack line and avoid stepping on crabs or disturbing nesting females.

animals.name: Giant Water Bug
animals.behavior_notes: Giant water bugs are ambush predators lurking in shallow freshwater ponds, marshes, and slow streams, becoming most active during warm months when prey is abundant. They are also strong fliers and are frequently attracted to lights at night during dispersal flights.
animals.viewing_tips: Shine a light over the surface of calm freshwater ponds or marshes at dusk to spot them near the surface. Check outdoor lights near water in summer, as they often fly to artificial light sources during nighttime dispersal.

animals.name: Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific octopuses emerge from rocky dens during cooler months to hunt crabs and fish in tidal zones. Spring months see increased foraging activity as water temperatures remain cold and food sources are plentiful.
animals.viewing_tips: Search rocky intertidal pools and kelp beds at low tide during dawn hours. Look for ink clouds or color-changing movements near crevices and overhanging rocks.

animals.name: Giant Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Giant Pacific Octopuses are most active in colder winter and early spring waters, emerging at dusk to hunt shellfish and fish. Females may be spotted guarding egg clutches in den cavities during this period.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling or scuba diving near rocky subtidal reefs offers the best chance of spotting these large cephalopods. Look for piles of crab and clam shells outside rocky dens, known as middens, which indicate an occupied site.

animals.name: Bioluminescent Dinoflagellates
animals.behavior_notes: Bioluminescent dinoflagellates produce a vivid blue glow when disturbed by wave action or movement during warm summer nights. Blooms intensify in calm, nutrient-rich bays during the warmest months of the year.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit a designated bioluminescent bay on a moonless night for the most dramatic effect. Kayaking or swimming gently through the water will trigger the blue flashes; avoid using sunscreen or bug spray which can harm the organisms.

animals.name: Jellyfish (Moon)
animals.behavior_notes: Moon jellyfish bloom in large aggregations along coastlines during summer months, drifting passively with currents. They are often carried into harbors and tidal coves where calm waters concentrate them.
animals.viewing_tips: Walk along piers, harbor docks, or calm coves during summer and scan the water surface — blooms can be spotted from shore without any special equipment. Early morning visits before wind picks up offer calmer water and better visibility.

animals.name: Dungeness Crab
animals.behavior_notes: Dungeness crabs migrate into shallower nearshore waters and estuaries during fall and early winter, making them more accessible to shore-based viewers. Males become particularly active searching for mates during this period.
animals.viewing_tips: Check sandy-bottomed tidal flats and estuaries at low tide during early morning hours. Crab traps set from piers in permitted areas can confirm presence, and rocky jetties often offer above-water viewing of crabs in shallow pools.

animals.name: American Lobster
animals.behavior_notes: American lobsters move into shallower inshore waters during summer as ocean temperatures rise, making them more accessible near rocky coastlines. They are nocturnal foragers, becoming most active from dusk through dawn.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling along rocky subtidal reefs at dusk gives the best chance of spotting lobsters in the wild. Look beneath boulders and inside crevices; they are rarely visible in open water during daylight.

animals.name: Coral (Elkhorn)
animals.behavior_notes: Elkhorn coral, a federally threatened species, forms its characteristic branching structures in shallow reef environments and is best observed during calm summer days when water clarity is highest. Spawning events can occur on specific nights following the August full moon.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling or shallow scuba diving in designated reef zones at Biscayne offers views of remaining Elkhorn colonies. Critically endangered — do not touch or anchor near coral; populations are severely reduced and require significant conservation effort to locate.

animals.name: Coral (Brain)
animals.behavior_notes: Brain corals are slow-growing massive corals found on Caribbean and Florida reef systems, most visible and vibrant in calm, clear summer waters. Their intricate maze-like surface patterns are best appreciated with good underwater visibility during midday light.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or dive along the Trunk Bay underwater trail at Virgin Islands National Park for reliable brain coral sightings. Visit on calm, sunny days between 10am–2pm for optimal water clarity and light penetration.

animals.name: Sea Anemone
animals.behavior_notes: Sea anemones are stationary filter feeders that extend their colorful tentacles during incoming tides to capture plankton, making spring tidal pools among the best places to observe their feeding behavior. They retract into compact blobs when exposed at low tide.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit rocky intertidal tidal pools during an incoming tide in the morning when anemones are fully extended and most colorful. Olympic National Park's Rialto Beach and Kalaloch tide pools are excellent accessible locations.

animals.name: Starfish (Sunflower Sea Star)
animals.behavior_notes: The Sunflower Sea Star, once among the most common large sea stars on the Pacific Coast, has been devastated by Sea Star Wasting Disease and is now critically endangered. Rare surviving individuals may be spotted in subtidal zones during spring and summer months.
animals.viewing_tips: Sightings are extremely rare due to population collapse from wasting disease — consider this a once-in-a-lifetime observation. Report any sightings to MARINe (Multi-Agency Rocky Intertidal Network) citizen science programs; scuba diving in subtidal zones offers the best but still unlikely chance.

animals.name: Pacific Sea Nettle
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific Sea Nettles bloom in large aggregations along the California coast during late summer, drifting with currents near the surface in calm, warm nearshore waters. Their long trailing tentacles and golden-brown bells are most visible from above on clear, calm days.
animals.viewing_tips: Look for aggregations from kayaks, whale-watching boats, or calm-water snorkel trips near Channel Islands. Early afternoon with flat seas and bright sunlight offers the best visibility into the water column.

animals.name: Mantis Shrimp
animals.behavior_notes: Mantis shrimp are most active at dawn and dusk, emerging from burrows in sandy or rubble-strewn reef areas to hunt. Spring months see increased activity as water temperatures rise, making them more likely to venture out and be spotted by snorkelers.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or dive shallow reef and rubble zones at Biscayne and look carefully into crevices and burrow openings — mantis shrimp blend well with substrate. A dive light used gently near holes can reveal their iridescent eyes peering back at you.
